metadata.methods_description: EEG was recorded with a 64-channel Synamps RT system (Neuroscan) at pre-, mid-, and post-test sessions. Participants sat in a darkened, electrically shielded chamber with impedance below 5 kΩ and the reference on the left mastoid. Vertical and horizontal EOG were recorded. The task was a distractor version of change detection with 2T0D, 4T0D, and 2T2D conditions.

citation_details.title: Working Memory Training in Norwegian Children with Cerebral Palsy (CP) Show Minimal Evidence of Near and No Far Transfer Effects
citation_details.author: Harald Beneventi, Gro C. Christensen Løhaugen, Guro Lillemoen Andersen, Cato Sundberg, Heidi Furre Østgård, Ellen Bakkan, Geir Walther, Torstein Vik, Jon Sverre Skranes
citation_details.abstract: ABSTRACT In children with cerebral palsy (CP), learning disabilities are well documented, and impairments in executive functions, such as attention, inhibition, shifting and working memory, represent significant burdens on patients, their families and the society. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether Cogmed RM working memory training could improve working memory in children with CP and investigate whether increased working memory capacity would generalize to other cognitive functions. Twenty-eight children completed the training and the results were compared to a waitlist control group (n = 32). The results yielded three main findings. First, children with CP improved with practice on trained working memory tasks. Second, the intervention group showed minimal near transfer effects to non-trained working memory tasks. Third, no effects on cognitive and behavioral far transfer measures were found.

citation_details.title: Effects of working memory span training on top-down attentional asymmetry at both neural and behavioral levels
citation_details.author: Yang Li, Xiongying Chen, Qiumei Zhang, Wending Xu, Jin Li, Jin Li, Feng Ji, Qi Dong, Chuansheng Chen, Jun Li, Jun Li
citation_details.abstract: The leftward asymmetry of the visual field and posterior brain regions, a feature of the normal attention process, can be strengthened by brain stimulation, e.g. administering alpha frequency stimulation to the left posterior cortex. However, whether it can be strengthened by cognitive training, especially with nonlateralized tasks, is unknown. We used a dataset from a 2-month-long randomized controlled trial and compared the control group with 2 training groups trained with backward or forward memory span tasks. A lateralized change detection task with varied memory loads was administered as the pre-, mid-, and post-tests with simultaneous electroencephalographic recording. Intrasubject response variability (IRV) and the alpha modulation index (MI) were calculated. Analysis of IRV showed more enhanced leftward attentional bias in the backward group than in the other groups. citation_details.title: Individual differences in working memory capacity predict the behavioral effects of induced eye movements in persuasion
citation_details.author: Arie Dijkstra, Hannah Schmidberger
citation_details.abstract: Objectives To study the role of the working memory (WM) in persuasion, eye movements (EMi) were induced during the processing of auditory persuasive information. EMi tax the WM and may thereby prevent defensive self-regulation. However, these effects may depend on individual differences in WM capacity. Method In an online experiment in Germany, WM capacity was assessed at pretest with the Forward and the Backward digit span, after which participants ( N = 230) were all exposed to an auditory persuasive message on fruit and vegetable consumption. Half of them were asked to follow with their eyes a neutral, horizontally regular moving stimulus on a screen (EMi condition). The dependent variable was self-reported fruit and vegetable consumption assessed after two weeks. citation_details.title: Saccadic System in Visuo-Spatial Working Memory and Visual Attention
citation_details.author: Sofia A. Mironets
citation_details.abstract: Working memory is a mechanism that maintains relevant information in an active, easily accessible state for mental analysis and behavioral control. While the cerebellum was long considered solely a motor center, its role in cognitive processes has only recently gained significant attention. There has been a lack of comprehensive research into the complex relationships between the theoretical construct of working memory, the functioning of visual attention, the anatomy of the saccadic system, and the specific role of the cerebellum in these processes. This analytical review examines neuroimaging, neuroanatomical, morphofunctional, and behavioral studies on the role of the saccadic system and the cerebellum in the neurophysiological support of visual attention and visuo-spatial working memory. citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.
